title: Phillips Petroleum Co. v. Shutts (1985)
summary: Kansas could bind the absent plaintiff class through the approved procedures, but could not automatically apply Kansas substantive law to all claims.
notes:
On remand, the Kansas court found no relevant conflict after examining the other states’ laws and reached the same practical result. That later result did not erase the Supreme Court’s requirement to perform the choice-of-law analysis.

Justice Rehnquist wrote for the Court; the class of roughly 33,000 royalty owners spanned all fifty states, and about 99% of the leases and 97% of the class members had no Kansas connection other than the suit; it was the defendant, Phillips, that raised the absent class members' due-process objection, and the Court allowed it standing to do so.

Rule statement: an absent plaintiff class member is bound if given adequate notice, an opportunity to be heard, a right to opt out, and adequate representation, so minimum contacts with the forum are not required; but a forum may apply its own law only if it has a significant contact or aggregation of contacts creating state interests, so the choice of law is not arbitrary or unfair.

sections.Parties: Royalty owners sued Phillips Petroleum for interest on delayed royalty payments and sought to represent similarly situated owners.
sections.Material Facts: The leases were located in eleven states. The proposed class of about 33,000 received mailed notice describing the suit, representation, participation, and the right to request exclusion. The final class exceeded 28,000 after exclusions and undeliverable notices. Almost all leases and most class members lacked a connection to Kansas apart from the litigation. Nevertheless, the Kansas court applied its own contract and equity law to every claim.
sections.Procedural History: The trial court entered a class judgment, and the Kansas Supreme Court affirmed. The United States Supreme Court affirmed jurisdiction over the plaintiff class but reversed the choice-of-law ruling and remanded.
sections.Issue: Did absent plaintiffs need the forum contacts required of defendants, and did jurisdiction permit Kansas to use its own law for all transactions?
sections.Holding: The absent plaintiffs did not need the same minimum contacts under the procedures provided. The blanket application of Kansas law, however, exceeded the constitutional limits identified by the Court.
sections.Reasoning: Absent class plaintiffs generally need not appear, hire counsel, defend counterclaims, or face coercive liability in the manner of defendants. Adequate representation and procedural safeguards could protect their claims without individual affirmative consent to the forum. For money damages or similar legal relief, the Court required appropriate notice, an opportunity to participate, a meaningful opt-out opportunity, and adequate representation. The choice-of-law question remained independent. Where material conflicts existed, the forum needed significant contacts creating interests in applying its law to the particular claims. The existence of a nationwide class did not create those substantive contacts or defeat the parties’ reasonable expectations about the law governing their leases.

learning.why: Kansas could bind the absent plaintiff class through the approved procedures, but could not automatically apply Kansas substantive law to all claims.

topics.cp-absent-plaintiffs: Absent damages claimants could be bound with adequate representation, notice, participation rights, and an opportunity to opt out.
topics.cp-personal-jurisdiction: The burdens on absent plaintiffs differed from those imposed on defendants compelled to defend.
topics.cp-choice-law: Jurisdiction over the class did not authorize automatic application of Kansas law to every claim.
topics.cp-class-notice: The mailed notice and meaningful exclusion procedure protected the absent claimants.
topics.cp-class-jurisdiction: Shutts defines when a court may bind absent plaintiff class members without minimum contacts.
topics.cp-due-process: Both holdings (binding absent plaintiffs and limiting choice of law) rest on the Due Process Clause.
topics.cp-class-actions: It is the leading Supreme Court decision on the constitutional footing of opt-out damages class actions.

learning.separateOpinions: Justice Stevens agreed with the jurisdiction analysis but dissented from the choice-of-law disposition. Justice Powell did not participate.
